sections.title: What is a Function in Python?

blocks.text: A function is a named, reusable block of code that does one job. You write the logic once, give it a name, and call that name whenever you need the job done again — instead of copy-pasting the same five lines into twelve different places in your script. That's the entire pitch, and it's the single biggest jump in code quality most beginners make once it actually clicks.

In Python, you define a function using the def keyword, give it a name, list whatever inputs it needs in parentheses, and indent the block of code that runs when it's called. Something like def calculate_discount(price, percent): followed by the logic underneath. Call it later with calculate_discount(500, 10) and Python runs that block with those specific values plugged in.

Here's the thing nobody tells you early enough: functions aren't really about avoiding repetition, even though that's how they're usually introduced. The real value shows up once your project grows past 200 lines and you can't hold the whole thing in your head anymore. A well-named function — send_confirmation_email(user) instead of forty lines of SMTP logic sitting inline — lets you read the calling code and understand what's happening without caring how it happens. That's the actual skill you're building here, not just syntax memorisation.

I once inherited a script where someone had written the same 15-line 'validate and format phone number' logic six separate times across the file, each slightly different because bugs got fixed in one copy and never propagated to the others. Two of the six copies had actual different behaviour by the time I found it — not intentionally, just drift. One function, called six times, would have made that impossible. This guide covers everything from a bare-minimum function definition to *args, **kwargs, scope rules, lambda functions, recursion, and the specific errors you'll hit along the way.

sections.title: History — How Python's Function Syntax Evolved

blocks.text: Functions have been core to Python since its very first release — this isn't a bolted-on feature, it's foundational. But the syntax around them has picked up real capability over the decades, and knowing the timeline helps when you're reading code from different eras.

items.text: — def, return, and basic positional parameters were present from Python's earliest public release. Functions were first-class citizens from day one — you could already pass them around as values, store them in variables, and pass them as arguments to other functions.
— Added lambda, along with map, filter, and reduce — bringing genuine functional-programming tools into the language, allowing small anonymous functions without a full def block.

— Introduced nested scopes properly, allowing inner functions to read variables from their enclosing function's scope (closures), which unlocked decorator patterns years before decorators had dedicated syntax.
— Introduced the @decorator syntax, letting one function wrap and modify another using a clean @ prefix rather than the old-style manual function = decorator(function) reassignment pattern.
— Enhanced generators with the ability to send values back into a generator function via .send(), laying groundwork for what eventually became async/await syntax.

— Added keyword-only arguments (parameters after a bare * in the signature) and function annotations (type hints on parameters and return values), both aimed at making function signatures more explicit and self-documenting.
— Introduced async def and await, extending function syntax to cover asynchronous coroutines as a distinct, first-class kind of function.

— Added positional-only parameters using a / in the signature, giving developers explicit control over whether an argument can be passed by keyword at all — useful for library authors who want to rename a parameter later without breaking callers.

— Function syntax is now genuinely rich: positional-only params, keyword-only params, defaults, *args, **kwargs, type hints, decorators, and async support all coexist in one coherent grammar. Most beginner code only ever touches a fraction of this — and that's fine, the basics haven't changed at all since 1991.

blocks.text: Python functions are more flexible than most beginners realise on day one. Here are the 12 characteristics that actually matter once you start writing real code:

items.title: Defined with def
items.text: Every function starts with def function_name(parameters):, followed by an indented block. The name should describe what the function does — get_user_age(), not do_stuff().

items.title: First-Class Objects
items.text: Functions in Python are values, exactly like integers or strings. You can assign them to variables, store them in lists, and pass them as arguments to other functions — this is what makes decorators and callbacks possible.

items.title: Optional return Statement
items.text: A function without an explicit return automatically returns None. This trips up beginners who forget the keyword and then wonder why result comes back as None instead of the value they computed.

items.title: Flexible Parameter Types
items.text: Positional, keyword, default-valued, *args (variable positional), and **kwargs (variable keyword) parameters can all combine in a single signature, in a specific required order.

items.title: Own Local Scope
items.text: Variables created inside a function exist only inside that function unless explicitly declared global. This isolation is what prevents functions from silently stepping on each other's variables.

items.title: Docstrings for Documentation
items.text: A string literal right after the def line — triple-quoted by convention — becomes the function's docstring, accessible via help(function_name) or function_name.__doc__.

items.title: Can Call Themselves (Recursion)
items.text: A function can call itself from within its own body. This is how recursive algorithms like factorial calculation or tree traversal get written in Python.

items.title: Anonymous Functions via lambda
items.text: lambda x: x * 2 creates a small, unnamed function in a single expression — useful for short throwaway logic passed to sort(), map(), or filter(), but limited to a single expression, no statements.

items.title: Type Hints (Optional)
items.text: def greet(name: str) -> str: annotates expected parameter and return types. Python doesn't enforce these at runtime — they're purely documentation for humans and tools like mypy.

items.title: async def for Coroutines
items.text: Adding async before def creates a coroutine function, meant to be awaited inside an event loop rather than called directly — the foundation of Python's asyncio concurrency model.

items.title: Nested Functions & Closures
items.text: Functions can be defined inside other functions, and the inner function can 'remember' variables from the outer function's scope even after the outer function has finished running.

items.title: No Function Overloading
items.text: Unlike Java or C++, Python doesn't support multiple functions with the same name but different parameter types. Defining a name twice simply replaces the earlier definition entirely.

sections.title: How a Function Call Executes — Flowchart

blocks.text: Calling a function isn't just 'jumping to some code.' Python does a specific sequence of steps every single time — binding arguments to parameters, creating a fresh local scope, running the body, and handing back whatever the return statement produces (or None if there isn't one). Here's that pipeline laid out precisely.

Key insight: step 3 — the fresh local scope — is exactly why a variable named price inside calculate_discount() has zero relationship with a variable named price sitting in your main script. Each call gets its own clean namespace, used once, then discarded. This is also why recursive functions don't confuse their own local variables between different levels of recursion — every call, no matter how deep, gets a brand new scope.

sections.title: How Functions Actually Work — Parameters, Arguments, and Return Values

blocks.text: Three concepts sit at the core of every function you'll write: the distinction between parameters and arguments (people use these words interchangeably in casual conversation, but they mean different things), how return actually works, and how default arguments quietly become one of Python's most infamous gotchas.
🏷️ Parameters vs Arguments — The Distinction That Actually Matters

A parameter is the name listed in the function definition: def greet(name): — name is the parameter. An argument is the actual value you pass when calling it: greet("Rohan") — "Rohan" is the argument. Interviewers ask this distinction specifically because it reveals whether someone actually understands function mechanics or has just been pattern-matching syntax. It's a small distinction, but it's precise, and precision here pays off once you start reading error messages that use these exact terms.
↩️ return — What It Actually Does

return does two things simultaneously: it immediately stops the function's execution — any code after it in that function never runs — and it hands a value back to whoever called the function. Forgetting return is one of the most common beginner mistakes: writing def add(a, b): print(a + b) instead of return a + b means the function prints the sum but gives back None to anything trying to use the result. Try result = add(3, 4) followed by result + 10 and you'll get TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int' — a genuinely confusing error the first time you see it, because the function looked like it worked fine when you ran it directly.
⚠️ The Mutable Default Argument Trap

This is Python's single most famous function-related gotcha, and it catches experienced developers too, not just beginners. Write def add_item(item, basket=[]): and the empty list [] is created exactly once — when the function is defined, not each time it's called. Every call that relies on the default shares the exact same list object. Call add_item("apple") then add_item("banana") with no second argument each time, and you'd expect two separate baskets — instead you get one basket containing both items, because they were both silently appending to the same shared list. The fix is the standard idiom: def add_item(item, basket=None): if basket is None: basket = []. This pattern shows up constantly in real code reviews.
🌐 Scope — Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in (LEGB)

Python resolves variable names using what's called the LEGB rule: it checks Local scope first (inside the current function), then Enclosing scope (any outer function it's nested inside), then Global scope (module-level), then Built-in scope (Python's own reserved names like len or print). A variable assigned inside a function is local by default — trying to modify a module-level variable from inside a function without the global keyword just creates a new local variable instead, which is a common source of confusion when a function seems to 'not update' a global value.

Simple rule to remember: parameters are names in the definition, arguments are values at the call site, return hands back a value and stops execution immediately, and default arguments should never be mutable objects like lists or dicts unless you genuinely want that sharing behaviour (which is rare).

sections.title: Defining Functions — Python vs Other Languages

blocks.text: Function syntax is one of the sharpest contrasts between Python and statically typed languages, and it explains a lot about why Python feels faster to prototype in but riskier to scale without discipline.

rows: Method inside a class (no standalone functions)

blocks.text: My honestly opinionated take: Python's decision to skip function overloading entirely is the right call for the language it is. Java needs overloading because its type system demands a separate method signature for every parameter-type combination. Python's default arguments plus *args/**kwargs combination covers nearly every real use case overloading solves in Java, with dramatically less boilerplate — one function, sensible defaults, done. The trade-off is that Python leans entirely on the developer's discipline to keep a function's behaviour coherent across all the ways it can be called, since there's no compiler enforcing separate, type-safe code paths for you.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Python Functions

blocks.text: Functions are close to a pure positive in software design, but Python's specific implementation has real trade-offs worth knowing.

pros.title: Eliminates Code Duplication
pros.text: Write logic once, call it everywhere it's needed. Fixing a bug means fixing it in exactly one place instead of hunting down every copy-pasted instance.

pros.title: Extremely Flexible Signatures
pros.text: Default arguments, *args, **kwargs, keyword-only, and positional-only parameters combined give Python function signatures remarkable expressive range without needing overloading.

pros.title: First-Class, Composable Values
pros.text: Passing functions as arguments to other functions (higher-order functions) enables clean patterns like sort(key=custom_function) or decorator-based behaviour injection.

pros.title: Self-Documenting via Docstrings and Type Hints
pros.text: help(function_name) and IDE tooltips pull directly from docstrings and annotations, making well-written functions genuinely self-explanatory to callers.

pros.title: Natural Fit for Testing
pros.text: Small, focused functions with clear inputs and outputs are exactly what unit testing frameworks like pytest are built to exercise efficiently.

pros.title: Supports Both Simple and Advanced Patterns
pros.text: The same def keyword scales from a two-line utility function all the way to async coroutines and recursive algorithms — no separate syntax needed for 'advanced' functions.

cons.title: No Compile-Time Type Checking
cons.text: A function expecting a number but receiving a string won't fail until that specific line actually runs, unlike statically typed languages that catch mismatches before the program ever executes.

cons.title: Mutable Default Argument Trap
cons.text: The shared-default-list gotcha is a genuine, repeated source of subtle bugs, especially for anyone coming from languages where default parameters are freshly created on every call.

cons.title: No Function Overloading
cons.text: You can't define two functions with the same name for different argument types the way Java or C++ allows — you have to handle type variation manually inside a single function body.

cons.title: Scope Rules Can Surprise Beginners
cons.text: Modifying a global variable from inside a function requires the explicit global keyword, and forgetting it silently creates an unrelated local variable instead of an error.

cons.title: Recursion Depth Limits
cons.text: Python's default recursion limit (typically 1000 calls deep) is comparatively low, and deep recursive algorithms can hit RecursionError where an iterative approach would have been safer.

cons.title: Performance Overhead of Function Calls
cons.text: Each function call in CPython carries real overhead compared to inlined code, which matters in genuinely hot loops — though this rarely matters until you're optimising something CPU-bound at scale.

blocks.text: Here's a function that looks reasonable, the exact error it produces when called incorrectly, and the corrected, properly defensive version.

lines: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int'

blocks.text: The bug: price - discount is computed but never returned — no return keyword means the function gives back None regardless. Here's the corrected version, with default arguments, a docstring, and basic validation:

blocks.label: robust_function.py
lines: """Return the price after applying a percentage discount.
float: Final price after discount is applied.
raise ValueError("price and percent must be non-negative")

blocks.text: Practice This Code — Live Editor

blocks.initialCode:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

print(greet("Ananya"))
print(greet("Rohan", greeting="Namaste"))

blocks.text: Line-by-Line Explanation

items.html: def calculate_discount(price, percent=10): — percent has a default value, making it optional. price has no default, so it remains required — every call must supply it.

"""...""" right after the def line — This is the function's docstring. It's not a comment; it's an actual string object accessible later via calculate_discount.__doc__ or Python's built-in help() function.

raise ValueError(...) — Validates inputs before doing any real work. This is defensive programming: catching bad input early with a clear error, rather than letting a nonsensical negative discount silently produce a nonsensical result.
return round(price - discount, 2) — The fix for the earlier bug. This line both computes AND hands back the final value, stopping the function immediately after.
calculate_discount(200) — Called with only one argument. Python uses the default percent=10 automatically since no second value was supplied.

sections.title: Where Functions Actually Matter — Real-World Applications

blocks.text: Functions aren't a classroom-only abstraction — they're the fundamental unit of organisation in every serious Python codebase, across every domain:

items.text: — In Django and Flask, every URL route ultimately maps to a function (or method) that receives a request and returns a response. Understanding parameters and return values directly translates into understanding how web frameworks route and respond to requests.

— TensorFlow and PyTorch code is built almost entirely from functions — preprocessing functions, loss functions, training-step functions — chained together. A model training script is fundamentally a sequence of well-named function calls.
— Every reusable ops script — backup_database(), send_alert(), cleanup_old_logs() — is a function with a clear job, called from a main() function that orchestrates the overall script flow.

— pytest and unittest are built around calling small, focused functions and asserting on their return values. Code that isn't broken into functions is, practically speaking, code that can't be unit tested at all.
— Pandas-heavy scripts typically define functions like clean_column(df, name) or compute_summary_stats(df) to keep data-cleaning logic readable and reusable across multiple datasets.

— Functions like hash_password(), verify_token(), and check_permissions() isolate security-critical logic into single, auditable, testable units rather than scattering security checks inline throughout a codebase.
— Pygame-based games are organised around functions like update_player_position(), check_collision(), and render_frame(), typically called repeatedly inside a main game loop.

— AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, and Azure Functions are literally named after this concept — a single Python function is the entire deployable unit, triggered by an event and returning a response.

sections.title: Why Functions Are the Real Turning Point in Learning Python

blocks.text: Variables, loops, and conditionals teach you syntax. Functions teach you how to actually design software. Here's why this topic deserves more attention than it usually gets:

items.strong: 🧠 It's the First Real Abstraction Skill
items.text: — Deciding what a function should do, what it should be named, and what it should return is genuine software design — the first point where 'writing code that runs' and 'writing code that's good' start to diverge.

— 'Write a function that...' is the opening line of an enormous share of coding interview questions. Fluency with parameters, defaults, and return values isn't optional for interview prep — it's the baseline.

items.strong: 🐛 It Eliminates a Whole Category of Bugs
items.text: — The copy-paste-and-forget-to-update-all-copies bug class disappears almost entirely once logic lives in one function called from multiple places instead of duplicated inline.

items.strong: 🧪 It's the Foundation of Testable Code
items.text: — Nothing in software engineering practice matters more directly to code quality than whether your logic is broken into small, testable, well-named functions.

items.strong: 🔧 It Unlocks Every Advanced Python Feature
items.text: — Decorators, generators, async/await, context managers — every one of these is built on top of function fundamentals. Shaky function understanding makes every subsequent topic harder than it needs to be.

items.strong: 🇮🇳 It's the Core Skill Tested in Indian Placement Drives
items.text: — Campus placement coding rounds and early technical interviews at Indian product and service companies alike lean heavily on 'write a function to solve X' problems — this is the single most rehearsed skill in that entire process.

sections.title: Special Kinds of Functions Worth Knowing

blocks.text: Beyond the standard def function, Python has several specialised function forms, each solving a specific, narrow problem:

items.text: — sorted(students, key=lambda s: s['marks']) creates a throwaway function inline, without a name, limited to exactly one expression. Great for short logic passed to sort(), map(), or filter(); a poor choice for anything requiring multiple statements or clarity.

— def factorial(n): return 1 if n == 0 else n * factorial(n - 1) solves a problem by breaking it into a smaller version of itself. Elegant for tree structures and mathematical definitions, but watch out for Python's default recursion limit and RecursionError on genuinely deep recursion.

items.strong: Generator Functions — yield Instead of return
items.text: — A function using yield instead of return produces values lazily, one at a time, pausing between each — ideal for processing large sequences without loading everything into memory at once.

— A function defined inside another function can 'close over' variables from the outer scope, remembering them even after the outer function has finished executing. This is the mechanism decorators are built on.

— Defined with async def and called with await inside an event loop, these functions can pause and resume, enabling concurrent I/O-bound operations like multiple simultaneous network requests without blocking threads.
— Any function that accepts another function as a parameter or returns one as a result. map(), filter(), and every decorator in Python are higher-order functions by this definition.

rows: General-purpose reusable logic, the default choice
Short, throwaway logic passed to sort/map/filter
Lazy iteration over large or infinite sequences
Decorators, factory functions producing customised functions
Concurrent I/O-bound operations (network calls, file access)

blocks.text: These come up in essentially every Python interview, from campus placements to mid-level backend screening rounds. Know these precisely, not approximately.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between a parameter and an argument in Python?
items.a: A parameter is the variable name listed in a function's definition — in def greet(name):, name is the parameter. An argument is the actual value supplied when the function is called — in greet('Priya'), 'Priya' is the argument. Parameters describe what a function expects; arguments are the concrete values given at each specific call.

items.q: Q2. What does a Python function return if it has no explicit return statement?
items.a: It returns None automatically. This surprises beginners who write a function that prints a computed value but forgets to return it — calling that function and trying to use the result then produces None instead of the expected value, often leading to a TypeError further down the line.

items.q: Q3. Explain the mutable default argument problem in Python with an example.
items.a: Default argument values are evaluated exactly once, when the function is defined — not on each call. def add_item(item, basket=[]): means every call relying on the default shares the same list object across calls, so items silently accumulate across unrelated calls instead of starting fresh each time. The standard fix is def add_item(item, basket=None): followed by if basket is None: basket = [] inside the function body.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between *args and **kwargs?
items.a: *args collects any extra positional arguments into a tuple — calling f(1, 2, 3) with def f(*args): gives args as (1, 2, 3). **kwargs collects any extra keyword arguments into a dictionary — calling f(name='Alice', age=30) with def f(**kwargs): gives kwargs as {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30}. Both can appear in the same signature, with *args always coming before **kwargs.

items.q: Q5. What does the LEGB rule mean in the context of Python variable scope?
items.a: LEGB describes the order Python searches when resolving a variable name: Local scope (inside the current function) first, then Enclosing scope (any outer function it's nested in), then Global scope (module level), then Built-in scope (Python's reserved names like len or print). Python stops at the first scope where it finds a matching name.

items.q: Q6. Why does modifying a global variable inside a function sometimes not work as expected?
items.a: Assigning to a variable inside a function makes it local by default, even if a global variable with the same name already exists. Writing count = count + 1 inside a function without declaring global count first raises UnboundLocalError, because Python treats count as a new local variable the moment it sees an assignment to it anywhere in that function body, and that local count hasn't been given a value yet at that line.

items.q: Q7. What's the difference between a regular function defined with def and a lambda function?
items.a: A lambda is restricted to a single expression with no statements, no multi-line logic, and no name of its own unless explicitly assigned to a variable. A def function can contain multiple statements, loops, conditionals, docstrings, and default arguments. lambda is meant for short, throwaway logic; def is the standard choice for anything with real complexity.

items.q: Q8. What error occurs if you call a function without providing all of its required positional arguments, and what does it look like exactly?
items.a: TypeError: function_name() missing 1 required positional argument: 'argument_name'. For example, calling calculate_discount(500) when the function is defined as def calculate_discount(price, percent): (with no default for percent) raises exactly this error, naming the specific missing parameter.

items.q: Q9. What is a closure in Python, and how does it relate to nested functions?
items.a: A closure occurs when an inner function, defined inside an outer function, references a variable from the outer function's scope, and that inner function is then returned or used after the outer function has finished executing. The inner function 'remembers' that outer variable even though the outer function's own execution has ended — this mechanism underlies how Python decorators work.

items.q: Q10. What is recursion, and what's the risk of writing a recursive function without a proper base case?
items.a: Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem, eventually stopping at a base case that returns a value directly without recursing further. Without a correct base case, or with a base case that's never actually reached, the function calls itself indefinitely until Python's recursion limit is hit, raising RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded.

blocks.text: Work through these before checking the answers. Predicting the exact output — or exact error message — is the real test of whether function mechanics have actually clicked.

items.q: 1. What is the output of: def f(): pass \n print(f())
items.a: None. The function body is just pass, which does nothing, and with no explicit return statement, Python automatically returns None — which is exactly what gets printed.

items.q: 2. What happens when you call greet() if the function is defined as def greet(name='World'): return f'Hello, {name}!'?
items.a: It returns 'Hello, World!'. Since name has a default value and the call supplies no argument, Python uses the default. Calling greet('Priya') instead would override the default and return 'Hello, Priya!'.

items.q: 3. Trace through this: def add_item(item, basket=[]): basket.append(item); return basket — then call add_item('apple') followed by add_item('banana'). What does the second call return?
items.a: ['apple', 'banana']. Because the default list is created only once at function definition time and shared across all calls that rely on the default, the second call appends to the exact same list the first call already modified, rather than starting with a fresh empty list.

items.q: 4. What's the exact error from calling def calculate(price, tax): return price + tax as calculate(100)?
items.a: TypeError: calculate() missing 1 required positional argument: 'tax'. Python names the specific missing parameter directly in the error message, which is genuinely useful for quickly identifying the fix.

items.q:
5. What does this print? def outer(): x = 10 
 def inner(): print(x) 
 inner() 
 outer()
items.a: 10. inner() is a closure over outer()'s local variable x — it can read x from the enclosing scope without needing it passed as a parameter, following the Enclosing step of the LEGB rule. Note this only works for reading x; modifying it inside inner() would require the nonlocal keyword.

items.q:
6. Why does this raise an error? def counter(): count = 0 
 def increment(): count += 1 
 increment() 
 counter()
items.a: UnboundLocalError: local variable 'count' referenced before assignment. count += 1 inside increment() is treated as an assignment to count, which makes Python consider count a local variable of increment() — but that local count has no value yet at the point it's being incremented, since the += reads it before assigning. The fix is adding nonlocal count inside increment() to explicitly reference the enclosing scope's variable.

items.q: 7. What is the output of: numbers = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]; print(sorted(numbers, key=lambda x: -x))?
items.a: [5, 4, 3, 1, 1]. The lambda negates each number before comparison, effectively reversing the usual ascending sort order into descending order, without needing a separate named function just for this one-off sorting rule.

items.q: 8. What happens if a recursive function like def countdown(n): print(n); countdown(n - 1) is called with countdown(5), and what's missing?
items.a: It's missing a base case — a condition that stops the recursion. It will keep calling itself with progressively smaller n values (5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2...) indefinitely, eventually raising RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded once Python's default recursion limit is hit. A correct version needs something like if n <= 0: return before the recursive call.

sections.title: Conclusion — Functions Are Where Programming Actually Starts

blocks.text: Everything before functions — variables, loops, conditionals — is vocabulary. Functions are where you start writing actual sentences, and eventually, actual arguments. The jump from 'a script that runs top to bottom' to 'a collection of well-named, well-tested, reusable functions calling each other' is the single biggest shift in how your code reads, how easily it's debugged, and how confidently other people (including future you) can work with it.

If you are a complete beginner, the priority is getting parameters, return values, and default arguments to feel automatic — not something you have to consciously think through every time. If you're moving toward real projects, the priority shifts to design: what should this function actually be responsible for, what should it be named, and what's the smallest, clearest interface it can expose to the rest of your code.

✅ def, parameters, return — get the basics automatic
✅ Default arguments — but never mutable defaults

blocks.text: The habit worth building from here: every time you write a function, ask what it's actually responsible for, in one sentence. If the sentence needs an 'and' in it — 'validates the input AND saves it to the database AND sends a confirmation email' — that's usually a sign the function should be three smaller functions instead of one large one. This single habit, more than any syntax detail in this guide, is what separates code that stays maintainable as a project grows from code that quietly turns into a mess six months in.

Functions are the smallest real unit of software design in Python. Get comfortable naming them well, scoping them tightly, and returning exactly what they promise — everything else in the language builds on top of this. 🐍

items.q: What is the difference between a function and a method in Python?
items.a: A function is a standalone block of reusable code, defined with def and called independently, like calculate_discount(500, 10). A method is a function that's defined inside a class and is called on an object of that class, like my_list.append(5) — the object it's called on (my_list here) is automatically passed as the first argument, conventionally named self.

items.q: Why does my Python function return None instead of the value I calculated?
items.a: This almost always means the function is missing an explicit return statement. Computing a value with an expression like price - discount on its own line does nothing useful if it isn't returned — Python discards that computed value and returns None by default at the end of the function, unless a return statement explicitly hands a value back.

items.q: What is the mutable default argument problem in Python, and how do I avoid it?
items.a: Default argument values like def f(items=[]): are created exactly once when the function is defined, not fresh on every call — so a mutable default like a list or dictionary gets silently shared and modified across unrelated calls that rely on it. The standard fix is using None as the default and creating the actual mutable object inside the function body: def f(items=None): if items is None: items = [].

items.q: What's the difference between *args and **kwargs in a Python function definition?
items.a: *args collects any extra positional arguments passed to the function into a tuple. **kwargs collects any extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. A function can accept both: def f(*args, **kwargs): — with *args always listed before **kwargs in the signature.

items.q: Can a Python function call itself, and what is this called?
items.a: Yes — this is called recursion. A recursive function calls itself with a smaller or simpler version of its original input, eventually reaching a base case that stops the recursion and returns a direct value. Recursion needs a correctly defined and genuinely reachable base case, or the function will call itself indefinitely until Python raises RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded.

items.q: Why do I get UnboundLocalError when trying to modify a variable from inside a function?
items.a: This happens when you assign to a variable inside a function (like count += 1) without first declaring it as global or nonlocal, and Python treats that assignment as creating a brand-new local variable rather than modifying the outer one — but since that local variable hasn't been assigned a value yet at the point of the += operation, referencing it raises UnboundLocalError. The fix is adding a global or nonlocal declaration for that variable name inside the function, depending on whether it lives at module level or in an enclosing function's scope.
